naturalness.evidence: “What were the two divisions going off duty on the Sabbath commanded to do?” is idiomatic English. “Going off duty” naturally describes a shift ending, and the options use direct, familiar action phrases such as “Visit the market” and “Rest at home.”

processing.evidence: Readers must connect “going off duty on the Sabbath” to “the two divisions” and understand those divisions as both receiving the command and carrying out the requested action. These are ordinary, manageable operations needed to identify the intended group. The short options introduce no substantial comparison or reference-tracking burden.

context_economy.evidence: There is no additional introductory framing. “The two divisions going off duty on the Sabbath” usefully identifies the group being asked about rather than adding unnecessary setup.

structure_assessments.reason: In “the two divisions going off duty on the Sabbath,” the modifier attaches naturally to “divisions,” and the time phrase specifies their duty transition. This identification is useful to the intended question and does not create avoidable modifier load.

“What were the two divisions … commanded to do?” uses a familiar passive question pattern. Readers can readily treat the divisions as the command recipients and the performers of the action; identifying the command giver is unnecessary.
